explanation: The posterior surface of the pons is bounded by the medullary striae at its base (marking the pontomedullary junction), the cerebral aqueduct superiorly at the apex, and the floor consisting of the medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area.
keyConcept: Posterior pons bounded by: medullary striae (base), cerebral aqueduct (apex), medial eminence/facial colliculus/vestibular area (floor).

explanation: The posterior midbrain displays four colliculi: two superior colliculi (involved in visual reflexes) and two inferior colliculi (involved in auditory reflexes), collectively forming the tectal plate or quadrigeminal plate.
keyConcept: Posterior midbrain: two superior and two inferior colliculi.

explanation: The fourth ventricle roof consists of two vela: the superior medullary velum (connecting the superior cerebellar peduncles) forms the upper roof, while the inferior medullary velum (with choroid plexus) forms the lower roof.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof: superior and inferior medullary vela.

explanation: The fourth ventricle floor has two parts: the pontine part contains the medial eminence, facial colliculus, and vestibular area; the medullary part contains the hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, and vestibular trigone.
keyConcept: Floor of fourth ventricle: pontine (medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area) and medullary (three trigones).

explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle consist of the superior cerebellar peduncle superiorly, the inferior cerebellar peduncle and gracile/cuneate tracts inferiorly, and the lateral recess extending toward the cerebellum.
keyConcept: Lateral boundaries: SCP above, ICP and dorsal columns below, lateral recess.

explanation: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle lies in the lower part of the roof, formed by the inferior medullary velum and tela choroidea where blood vessels invaginate the pia mater.
keyConcept: Choroid plexus of fourth ventricle lies in lower roof.

explanation: General somatic efferent (GSE) cranial nerve nuclei include the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), abducent (CN VI), and hypoglossal (CN XII) nuclei supplying extraocular and tongue muscles.
keyConcept: GSE column nuclei: CN 3, 4, 6, 12.

explanation: Special visceral efferent (SVE) nuclei include the motor nucleus of trigeminal (CN V), motor nucleus of facial (CN VII), and nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X, XI) supplying branchial arch-derived muscles.
keyConcept: SVE column nuclei: motor nuclei of CN 5, 7, and nucleus ambiguus (9,10,11).

explanation: General visceral efferent (GVE) nuclei include the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (CN III for pupil constriction), superior salivatory (CN VII), inferior salivatory (CN IX), and dorsal vagal nuclei (CN X).
keyConcept: GVE column nuclei: Edinger-Westphal, superior/inferior salivatory, dorsal vagal.

explanation: The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, which are responsible for head movement and shoulder elevation.
keyConcept: Spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

explanation: The spinal accessory nerve originates from the spinal nucleus located in the ventral horn of the first five cervical segments (C1-C5), with fibers ascending through the foramen magnum to join the cranial root.
keyConcept: Spinal accessory originates from ventral horn of upper 5 cervical segments.

explanation: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve supplies the four muscles of mastication plus tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and the anterior belly of digastric.
keyConcept: Motor V supplies mastication muscles, tensor tympani/palate, mylohyoid, anterior digastric.

explanation: The medulla receives blood from the anterior spinal artery, PICA (the largest branch), and direct medullary branches of the vertebral artery, with additional contribution from posterior spinal arteries.
keyConcept: Medulla supplied by anterior spinal, PICA, vertebral branches, and posterior spinal arteries.

explanation: The pons is primarily supplied by paramedian and circumferential branches of the basilar artery, which penetrate the ventral surface to supply pontine nuclei and fibers.
keyConcept: Pons supplied by branches of basilar artery.

explanation: Pontine hemorrhage typically damages bilateral corticospinal and autonomic pathways, causing pinpoint pupils (loss of pupillary light reflex), hyperpyrexia (autonomic dysregulation), and quadriplegia.
keyConcept: Pontine hemorrhage: pinpoint pupils, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia.

explanation: The midbrain receives blood from branches of the posterior cerebral artery (supplying the anterior and lateral regions) and branches of the superior cerebellar artery (supplying the posterior region).
keyConcept: Midbrain supplied by posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.

explanation: Medial medullary syndrome (from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or vertebral artery) causes contralateral spastic hemiplegia below the lesion, contralateral loss of proprioception and fine touch, and ipsilateral flaccid tongue paralysis.
keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiplegia, proprioception loss, ipsilateral tongue palsy.

explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome from PICA occlusion) causes ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, hoarseness, and Horner syndrome.
keyConcept: Lateral medullary syndrome: ipsilateral face, contralateral body sensory loss, ataxia, Horner syndrome.

explanation: Anterior cranial fossa fractures typically tear the cribriform plate, causing CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia; blood tracks into orbital contents producing subconjunctival hemorrhage and orbital ecchymosis.
keyConcept: Anterior fossa fracture: CSF rhinorrhea, subconjunctival and orbital hemorrhage.

explanation: Middle cranial fossa fractures frequently involve the petrous temporal bone, causing CSF otorrhea, Battle sign (mastoid bruising), and commonly affecting CN VII and VIII with facial paralysis and hearing loss.
keyConcept: Middle fossa fracture: CSF otorrhea, Battle sign, CN 7 and 8 involvement.

explanation: Posterior cranial fossa fractures allow blood to escape into the nape of neck and posterior triangle due to gravity, presenting with mastoid and neck bruising that tracks inferiorly.
keyConcept: Posterior fossa fracture: blood tracks to nape and posterior triangle of neck.

explanation: The falx cerebri attaches superiorly to the crista galli and frontal crest, posteriorly to the tentorium's upper surface, along its upper border to the sagittal sulcus lips, and its free lower border encloses the inferior sagittal sinus.
keyConcept: Falx cerebri attachments: crista galli, tentorium, sagittal sulcus, inferior sagittal sinus.

explanation: The falx cerebelli attaches along its base to the tentorium cerebelli, at its apex to the foramen magnum margins, along its posterior border to the internal occipital crest, and is free anteriorly.
keyConcept: Falx cerebelli: tentorium base, foramen magnum apex, occipital crest posteriorly, free anteriorly.

explanation: The dura mater receives sensory innervation differently in each fossa: anterior fossa from anterior ethmoidal and maxillary nerves, middle fossa from maxillary and mandibular divisions, posterior fossa from meningeal branches of CN X, XII and C1-3.
keyConcept: Dura innervation: anterior (V1,V2), middle (V2,V3), posterior (CN 10,12, C1-3).

explanation: Dural venous drainage occurs via meningeal veins (accompanying meningeal arteries) and diploic veins (within skull bones), which connect to both intracranial venous sinuses and external scalp veins.
keyConcept: Dura drains via meningeal veins and diploic veins.

explanation: Extradural hemorrhage results from middle meningeal artery rupture causing arterial bleeding with rapid accumulation and lucid interval, while subdural hemorrhage involves bridging veins causing slower venous accumulation.
keyConcept: Extradural: arterial (meningeal); Subdural: venous (bridging veins).

explanation: The single (unpaired) dural venous sinuses include the superior sagittal, inferior sagittal, straight, and occipital sinuses, each lying in specific dural folds or along bone margins.
keyConcept: Single sinuses: superior sagittal, inferior sagittal, straight, occipital.

explanation: The paired dural sinuses include sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior petrosal, inferior petrosal, sigmoid, and transverse sinuses, occurring on both sides of the cranial cavity.
keyConcept: Paired sinuses: sphenoparietal, cavernous, superior/inferior petrosal, sigmoid, transverse.

explanation: The superior sagittal sinus receives tributaries from the superior cerebral veins, which drain the cerebral convexity, and communicates with arachnoid granulations that absorb CSF into venous blood.
keyConcept: SSS tributaries: superior cerebral veins and arachnoid villi.

explanation: The cavernous sinus is related anteriorly to the superior orbital fissure, posteriorly to the petrous apex and crus cerebri, medially to the pituitary gland and sphenoid sinus, laterally to the temporal lobe, superiorly to the optic tract and ICA, and inferiorly to foramen lacerum.
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus relations: orbital fissure anterior, petrous apex posterior, pituitary medially, temporal lobe laterally.

explanation: Within the cavernous sinus run the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic division of trigeminal, maxillary division of trigeminal, and abducent nerves, along with the internal carotid artery.
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus contents: CN 3,4,5V1,5V2,6, and internal carotid artery.

explanation: The cavernous sinus receives blood from the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins (connecting with facial venous drainage), the central retinal vein, and the superficial middle cerebral vein.
keyConcept: Cavernous tributaries: superior/inferior ophthalmic, central retinal, superficial middle cerebral veins.

explanation: The cavernous sinus drains posteriorly via the superior petrosal sinus (to sigmoid sinus) and inferior petrosal sinus (to jugular bulb), providing outflow from the cranial venous system.
keyConcept: Cavernous sinus drains via superior and inferior petrosal sinuses.

explanation: The cavernous sinus communicates with the pterygoid plexus via emissary veins through the foramen ovale, with the facial vein via the superior ophthalmic vein, and with the opposite cavernous sinus via the intercavernous sinuses.
keyConcept: Cavernous communications: pterygoid plexus, facial vein, opposite cavernous sinus.

explanation: The olfactory nerve (CN I) consists of special sensory fibers that pierce the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to reach the olfactory bulb from the nasal mucosa, making it unique among cranial nerves.
keyConcept: Olfactory nerve pierces cribriform plate to reach olfactory bulb.
